summary: This document adds an NNTP extension for authentication, letting a client pick a method, run an authentication exchange and optionally set up a security layer. It formalizes AUTHINFO USER/PASS from RFC 2980, deprecates two older methods, and defines a SASL profile for NNTP.

plainLanguage.summary: To read a private newsgroup you must show who you are. This sets the rules for the news server asking for a name and password, or other proof, in a standard way.

subtitle: How a Usenet news client proves who it is: the AUTHINFO command, with a password option and a SASL option.

tldr.problem: NNTP servers often need to know who a client is, to limit resource use, trace abusive posters or protect local newsgroups. The existing ad-hoc AUTHINFO USER/PASS commands were weak but widely used.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTHINFO extension formalizes AUTHINFO USER/PASS, restricted to use under a strong encryption layer, and adds AUTHINFO SASL so NNTP can use any SASL mechanism and optionally negotiate a security layer.
tldr.outcome: AUTHINFO SASL replaces the deprecated AUTHINFO GENERIC and SIMPLE methods. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2980 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4643 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2980 and has not been obsoleted. It sits beside the NNTP base specification, RFC 3977, and the TLS extension, RFC 4642.

sections.title: Why NNTP Needs Authentication
sections.content:
NNTP has traditionally given public access to newsgroups, but authentication is often useful: to control resource consumption, to identify abusers of the POST command, and to restrict access to "local" newsgroups.

The older AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS commands, documented in RFC 2980, are a very weak mechanism but are in widespread use. They are formalized here, but only for use with appropriate security layers. AUTHINFO GENERIC is deprecated in favor of a new AUTHINFO SASL command, so NNTP can reuse mechanisms built for other SASL-enabled protocols such as SMTP, POP, IMAP, LDAP and BEEP.

The RFC is read together with the NNTP base specification, RFC 3977. If the two conflict, the base specification wins unless this document says otherwise. Authorization (what an authenticated user may do) is site policy and is not covered.
sections.plainLanguage: Some news servers want to know who is asking, like a clubhouse that checks a membership card. This RFC writes down the rules for showing the card.

sections.title: Advertising and Using the AUTHINFO Extension
sections.content:
A server advertises the AUTHINFO capability in its reply to CAPABILITIES, with arguments saying which commands it offers. USER means AUTHINFO USER/PASS is available. SASL means AUTHINFO SASL is available, and the server must then also advertise a SASL capability listing its mechanism names. A server must implement at least one of the two to advertise the label, and may list AUTHINFO with no arguments to say that no authentication command is allowed right now.

The USER argument must not be advertised, and the commands should not be provided, unless a strong encryption layer such as TLS is in use (or backward compatibility dictates otherwise). Clients must ignore arguments they do not recognize.

A server answers a protected command with 480 to say the client must authenticate. A client may also start authentication at any time without a 480, and servers should accept that. A server must never reply to an AUTHINFO command itself with 480. A client must not continue past the first step unless the server answers with a 38x code.

After successful authentication the client must not issue another AUTHINFO command or MODE READER. The server stops advertising AUTHINFO and MODE-READER and rejects further AUTHINFO commands with 502. It must keep advertising the same SASL mechanism list, which lets a client spot an active down-negotiation attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The server posts a sign listing which ways you can prove who you are. Once you are checked in, you cannot check in again, and the sign comes down.

sections.title: AUTHINFO USER and PASS
sections.content:
These commands send a clear-text username and password. The client sends AUTHINFO USER first. If the server needs a password it answers 381, and the client then sends AUTHINFO PASS. Success is 281, failure is 481, and a command sent out of order gets 482. Note that 381 breaks the usual rule for 3xx codes: it means the client must use AUTHINFO PASS to finish.

If the server needs only a username, it must not send 381 and must answer a later AUTHINFO PASS with 482. The server must use the most recent AUTHINFO USER argument, and may require the password in the very next command. These commands must not be pipelined.

Because the password is exposed to anyone on the network path, an implementation must not offer AUTHINFO PASS without also supporting TLS. Using it without a strong encryption layer is deprecated, and implementations should be configurable to disable it then, with that as the default. Code 483 tells the client the connection is not secure enough.

A server may allow white space in usernames and passwords, but it may also split arguments at white space and lose the exact spacing. Clients should warn users whose credentials contain white space, and SASL PLAIN is recommended as the alternative.

If authentication fails, the client may carry on without it, try another mechanism, or send different credentials with another AUTHINFO command.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the doorman your name, then your secret word. The RFC says to whisper the secret word only through a sealed tube, because shouting it lets everyone hear.

sections.title: AUTHINFO SASL
sections.content:
This command is the NNTP profile of SASL. Its syntax is AUTHINFO SASL mechanism [initial-response]. The SASL service name is nntp. An unsupported mechanism gets 503; a mechanism that needs an encryption layer first gets 483.

The exchange is a series of server challenges and client responses, all Base64-encoded. A challenge arrives as a 383 reply with one argument. A zero-length challenge or response is sent as a single =. The client cancels by sending a line with a single asterisk, and the server then replies 481. The server finishes with 281, or 283 when the mechanism returns extra success data. A bad Base64 string gets 504, and an initial response given to a mechanism that does not support one gets 482.

An optional initial response saves a round trip. Because Base64 data can be long, the command may exceed 512 octets and the initial-response argument may exceed 497 octets, and servers must handle the largest size their mechanisms can produce. A client may omit the initial response if it would push the command past 512 octets.

The authorization identity is a simple username, and both sides must prepare it with SASLprep. For interoperability, implementations must implement DIGEST-MD5. If both USER/PASS and SASL are offered, SASL PLAIN should also be implemented, and it is preferred over AUTHINFO USER even without a strong encryption layer, because it avoids the white-space limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the doorman and you pass notes back and forth in a secret code until he is sure it is you. You can stop at any time by writing a star.

sections.title: Security Layers After Authentication
sections.content:
A SASL exchange may also set up a security layer for the rest of the session. For the client it starts with the octet right after the CRLF of its last response. For the server it starts right after the CRLF of its success reply.

When it takes effect, NNTP resets to the state just after the initial greeting, except that any effect of an earlier MODE READER stays. The server must discard everything it learned from the client (such as the current newsgroup and article number), and the client should discard and must not rely on what it learned from the server, such as the capability list. If both TLS and a SASL layer are active, the data is encoded by SASL first and then by TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you are checked in, you both start talking in a new private code, and everything said before the code started is forgotten so no one can trick you with it.

sections.title: Security and Logging
sections.content:
Anything exchanged before SASL negotiation may have been sent in the clear and altered by an active attacker, so sensitive knowledge from that time must be discarded once a security layer is established. CAPABILITIES should be re-issued and other state re-negotiated.

Implementations must support a configuration where mechanisms open to passive eavesdropping (AUTHINFO USER/PASS and SASL PLAIN) are not advertised or used without an external security layer such as TLS, and that should be the default. Because an active attacker can push a negotiation down to the weakest mechanism, clients and servers should be configurable to forbid weak mechanisms. A server may drop the connection after repeated failures, but not before at least 3 failed attempts.

Section 5 adds non-protocol advice: the authenticated identity should be recorded in an audit trail tied to articles posted, for example in headers or a log, and this should be the default. Servers may offer a way to turn this off because some people consider it a privacy violation.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not say the secret word where eavesdroppers can hear, and do not let anyone trick you into using the weakest lock. A server may write down who posted what.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the SASL/GSSAPI service name nntp, meaning authenticated use of Usenet news over NNTP. The RFC also gives the formal definition of the AUTHINFO extension for the NNTP extensions registry: the capability label is AUTHINFO with optional arguments USER and SASL, plus the SASL label for the mechanism list.

It defines three commands (AUTHINFO USER, AUTHINFO PASS, AUTHINFO SASL) and the new response codes 281, 283, 381, 383, 481 and 482. AUTHINFO commands cannot be pipelined.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also signs the official list book so everyone agrees on the names and numbers it uses.
